subject: Archaeology
title: Context Sheets: The Paper Trail
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Context Sheets: The Paper Trail.

hook.text: Every single layer of soil on a dig gets its own paper form. Some excavations generate thousands of these sheets.

buildup.text: Context sheets record soil color, texture, depth, contents, relationships to other layers, and interpretation.

discovery.text: Without these records, artifacts become meaningless objects. A Roman coin on its own tells far less than a coin in context.

twist.text: Some 19th-century excavations kept no records at all. Priceless objects sit in museums with no idea where they were.

climax.text: Digital recording is replacing paper. Tablets on-site let data flow straight to databases.

punchline.text: A coin in a museum is a curiosity. A coin with context is evidence.

quiz.question: Why are context sheets essential in archaeology?
options: They prove legal ownership of all artifacts found on the site
They record where every find came from — without context, artifacts lose their meaning
They are required for insurance purposes in case of site damage

details.summary: Context sheets are standardized recording forms completed for every identifiable deposit, cut, or structure during an excavation. Each context — a layer of soil, a wall, a pit fill — receives a unique number and is described, drawn, photographed, and related to adjacent contexts.
details.whyItMatters: Since excavation destroys what it studies, context sheets are the permanent record that replaces the physical site. Without them, an excavation produces objects but no understanding of how those objects relate to each other.
takeaways: Every deposit and feature gets a unique context number and record
Context sheets describe soil, relationships, and interpretation
They form the permanent archive replacing the destroyed site

faq.question: What information does a context sheet contain?
faq.answer: Context number, type (deposit, cut, or structure), physical description (color, texture, compaction, inclusions), dimensions, stratigraphic relationships (above, below, cut by, same as), interpretation, photographs, and the excavator's name and date. Some add soil sample and finds details.

faq.question: Why is single-context recording considered best practice?
faq.answer: Recording each deposit individually ensures no information is lost. Older methods that grouped layers together lost fine-grained stratigraphic detail. Single-context recording, developed in the 1970s, allows precise reconstruction of site formation sequences from the paper record.
